topic.title: How a melted candy bar beside a radar tube led to the microwave oven

title: How Did a Melted Candy Bar Invent the Microwave?
description:
How did a melted candy bar give us the microwave oven?
Percy Spencer, a Raytheon engineer, was testing a radar tube when the chocolate in his pocket melted. We build the tube in 3D and show how it heats your food.
Sources: History.com (Jan 1947).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.

topic.title: How Hoover Dam turns the push of Lake Mead into electricity, and why a lower lake cuts it

title: Why Does Hoover Dam Need Lake Mead to Be Full?
description:
Why does Hoover Dam need Lake Mead to be full?
We cut the dam open in 3D: the intake towers, the pipes, the turbine and the spinning magnets, and why the height of Lake Mead decides how much power it makes.
Sources: US Bureau of Reclamation (May 2026).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.

topic.title: How the first transistor, two gold contacts on a plastic wedge at Bell Labs, became the switch inside every chip

title: What Did the First Transistor Actually Look Like?
description:
What did the first transistor actually look like?
At Bell Labs in December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain pressed two gold contacts onto a piece of germanium. We build it in 3D, show how it amplifies, then dive into a modern graphics chip built from the same switch.
Sources: Computer History Museum, NVIDIA GeForce News (Sep 2022).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.

topic.title: How a Crossrail tunnel boring machine dug the Elizabeth line under London, lining the tunnel as it went, and passed a working Tube line

title: How Did Crossrail Tunnel Past the Tube?
description:
How did Crossrail dig a new railway through ground already full of Tube tunnels?
We walk a 150-metre tunnel boring machine from its spinning cutterhead to the arm that builds the tunnel's concrete rings behind it, then show how close it came to the Northern line.
Sources: Arup (Nov 2026).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.

topic.title: How Motorola's team built the first handheld mobile phone in six weeks for a 1973 demo, then took ten more years to sell one

title: Why Was the First Mobile Phone a Brick?
description:
Why was the first phone you could carry, Motorola's, the size of a brick?
We build the 1973 prototype part by part in 3D, follow it to the street demo in New York, then stand the first phone you could buy beside the one in your hand.
Sources: Motorola Solutions, Guinness World Records (Nov 2026).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.

topic.title: How Starlink's Flat Dish Aims at Satellites Without Moving

title: How Does Starlink's Flat Dish Aim Without Moving?
description:
How does Starlink's flat dish follow satellites racing across the sky without ever turning?
We follow one signal from your laptop up to a Starlink satellite and back, open the dish in 3D, and draw its phased array wave by wave: how many tiny antennas firing a fraction apart bend a beam with no motor.
Then the handoff, when your satellite sets and the next one rises, and how the network grew from its first launch.

Sources: Space.com, Starlink, Wikipedia (Geostationary orbit, Starlink), Nov 2026.

topic.title: Why some Paris Metro lines roll on rubber tyres, and the steel wheels hidden behind them in case one goes flat

title: Why Does the Paris Metro Run on Rubber Tyres?
description:
How does a Paris Metro train on rubber tyres stay on the track?
We cut a rubber-tyred bogie open in 3D: the tyres on flat tracks, the sideways guide wheels, and the steel wheels waiting behind them, then follow the idea from Michelin's 1931 railcar to Montreal.
Sources: Michelin Metro (Nov 2026).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.

topic.title: How a Chip Factory Prints Billions of Switches With Light

title: How Does ASML's EUV Machine Print a Chip With Light?
description:
How does a machine print the chip in your phone with light, line by line, finer than anything a lens can focus?
We follow the light through ASML's EUV machine in 3D: molten tin drops hit twice by a laser, a glowing plasma, a row of mirrors in a vacuum, a patterned mask, and the silicon wafer below it.
Then the newest High-NA machine that prints even finer lines, and how the switches of a chip are built up, layer after layer.

Sources: ASML (Nov 2026).

topic.title: How NVIDIA's first chip, the NV1, drew 3D with curved patches instead of triangles, lost to DirectX's triangles, and how the triangle chip that followed saved the company

title: What Was Wrong With NVIDIA's First Chip?
description:
Why did almost no game use NVIDIA's first graphics card?
We build its chip in 3D and set its curved patches beside the triangles every other chip drew, then follow how DirectX settled the fight and what NVIDIA built next.
Sources: Jon Peddie Research, SiliconANGLE (Jan 2026).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.

topic.title: Why the school answer for how a wing lifts a plane is wrong, and how an A380's wing really holds it up

title: Why Does This Wing Lift Airbus's Superjumbo?
description:
Why does a wing actually lift Airbus's double-decker superjumbo off the ground?
We follow two puffs of air over an Airbus superjumbo wing in 3D, show why the top one does not wait for the bottom one, and what really pushes the wing up.
Sources: Airbus (Feb 2022), NASA Glenn Research Center.
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.
